info.name: Brainixa — Store: Products & Categories
info.description:
The store's products and their categories.

SPLIT BY WHO CALLS IT:

  admin/  — creating, pricing and filing products. Needs `admin_token` and the
            `manage_products` permission.
  user/   — the shop front. Auth is optional on /store and not used at all on
            the two public reads.

SETUP

  1. Import `brainixa_postman_environment.json` and pick "Brainixa - Live".
  2. Sign in as an admin and put the access token in `admin_token`.
  3. Run admin/Product Categories → Create first: it stores the new id in
     `product_category_id`, which the product requests then use. Create product
     does the same for `product_id`.

So the folders run top to bottom without a single id pasted by hand.

NEEDS MIGRATIONS 127 AND 128. Without 127 the product endpoints report that the
table is missing and /store quietly returns only books — a half-deployed server
should still have a shop. Without 128 a product simply has no attachment.

NOT HERE: buying. This is the catalogue — the tables, the admin screens and the
shop front. Checkout is its own piece of work and has not been built.

item.name: admin
item.description:
Everything behind the dashboard. Every request here needs `admin_token` and the
`manage_products` permission — which is separate from `manage_books` on purpose:
whoever prices the school bags is not necessarily whoever uploads the PDFs.

item.name: Product Categories
item.description: The store's own categories. Run Create first — it fills `product_category_id`.

query.description: Matches the code or any translated name.

request.description:
Product categories, each with `products_count`.

These are the STORE's categories, not the courses'. "School Bags" is not a course category and the two lists are deliberately separate.

Permission: `manage_products`.

One category with its translations.

Permission: `manage_products`.

Creates a category and stores this request's id in `product_category_id`.

At least one of `name_ar` / `name_en` is required. `code` is generated from the name when omitted — including from an Arabic-only name, which an older generator used to collapse to a single dash.

`image` also accepts a URL, a stored path, or a base64 data URI.

Permission: `manage_products`.

body.raw:
{
    "name_ar": "حقائب مدرسية",
    "name_en": "School Bags",
    "description_ar": "حقائب وشنط للطلاب",
    "description_en": "Bags and backpacks for students",
    "order_num": 1,
    "is_active": 1
}

exec: console.warn("No id in the response:", body?.message);

request.description:
Only the fields present in the body are written. Everything else is left alone.

Permission: `manage_products`.

Deletes the category. THE PRODUCTS SURVIVE — `product_category_id` is ON DELETE SET NULL, so the shelf is emptied rather than the stock on it destroyed.

The response reports `uncategorised_products`, because "deleted" on a screen listing 40 products should not leave you guessing whether the 40 went with it.

Permission: `manage_products`.

item.name: Products
item.description: Create fills `product_id`, which the rest of the folder uses.

query.description: Matches name, description, slug or SKU.
Applied to the EFFECTIVE price, so a product on sale is filtered at what it actually costs.
Only products that can be bought (stock null or above zero).
Filter by status. Admin only — the store never shows inactive products.

request.description:
All products, active and not.

`statistics` carries the total / active / inactive / out-of-stock counts.

Permission: `manage_products`.

One product with its translations, its category and its attachment.

Unlike the store, this always returns `file_path` — the admin owns the file regardless of `file_is_public`.

Permission: `manage_products`.

Creates a product and stores its id in `product_id`.

TWO FIELDS MEAN MORE THAN THEY LOOK:

  sale_price   null = not on sale    0 = deliberately free
  stock        null = not tracked    0 = out of stock

Sending 0 for a field you meant to leave blank marks the product free and sold out. Omit them instead.

A `sale_price` above `price` is refused. `effective_price`, `is_on_sale`, `discount_percent` and `is_stock_tracked` come back computed — a sale price that each screen applies for itself is one they eventually disagree about.

`slug` is generated from the name when omitted, Arabic included, and walks to `-2` on a clash.

Permission: `manage_products`.

body.raw:
{
    "name_ar": "حقيبة مدرسية ظهر",
    "name_en": "School Backpack",
    "description_ar": "حقيبة ظهر مقاومة للماء",
    "description_en": "Water-resistant backpack",
    "product_category_id": "{{product_category_id}}",
    "sku": "BAG-001",
    "price": 450,
    "sale_price": 360,
    "currency": "EGP",
    "stock": 12,
    "is_active": 1,
    "show_on_website": 1,
    "order_num": 1
}

exec: console.warn("No id in the response:", body?.message);

request.description:
The smallest body that works: a name and a price.

No category (uncategorised), no sale price (not on sale), no stock (not tracked, so it never reads as sold out).

Permission: `manage_products`.

Only the fields present in the body are written.

BOTH prices are resolved to what they WILL be after the update and checked against each other once. Sending `price` alone, below a sale price already stored, is refused — otherwise the discount would cost more than the product, and lowering a price is the ordinary way that happens.

To clear the sale price send `"sale_price": null`. To stop tracking stock send `"stock": null`.

Permission: `manage_products`.

Flips `show_on_website` and returns the result. The same one-click toggle courses and books have.

A hidden product stays in the admin list and disappears from `/store`.

Permission: `manage_products`.

Permanent. Its translations go with it (ON DELETE CASCADE).

Permission: `manage_products`.

item.name: Product Files
item.description: Attaching a file of ANY type, and the two requests that prove the guard works.

formdata.description: ANY file type. Pick one from disk — .dwg, .ttf, .apk, .7z, .stl, anything that is not executable.
0 = only the admin gets the path. 1 = the store serves it to anyone.

request.description:
Creates a product WITH a file, as multipart — which is how the dashboard sends a real upload.

ANY extension is accepted EXCEPT what a web server might run: php, phtml, exe, sh, jar, htaccess and the rest. Every segment of the name is checked, so `invoice.pdf.php` is refused as well as `shell.php`.

The name on disk is always generated; the name you uploaded is stored separately and used only for the download and the screen.

If the file is refused the PRODUCT IS STILL CREATED, and the message says why — look for `data.file_warning`.

Permission: `manage_products`.

The JSON way to attach a file: a base64 data URI of ANY media type.

SEND `file_name`. Without it the extension is guessed from the mime subtype, and guessing an extension from a subtype is exactly the hole that once let "data:image/php;base64,..." write a webshell — so the subtype is a last resort and is run through the same deny-list.

Ceiling: 25 MiB decoded. Apache also caps the whole request at 20 MiB, so 20 MiB is the real limit.

Permission: `manage_products`.

Hands the download link to the shop front.

Default is 0 — NOT public — because a product file may well BE the thing being sold, and there is no checkout yet to gate it behind. Set 1 for something meant for everyone, like a spec sheet.

Permission: `manage_products`.

An explicit null removes the attachment.

An ABSENT `file` means "keep the one it has" — the two are told apart, so saving a product after editing its price does not wipe its file.

Permission: `manage_products`.

Here to be run, not avoided: it SHOULD fail.

Expect the product to save and the message to say the file was refused. Try `invoice.pdf.php` too — the double extension is refused the same way.

If a file like this ever lands in uploads/, something is wrong: say so rather than working around it.

item.name: user
item.description:
The shop front, as a student or a signed-out visitor sees it.

/store takes an optional student token: remove the Authorization header and it
still answers. The other two take none at all.

query.description: A PRODUCT category. Books have none, so passing this excludes them — the response says so in applied_filters.books_excluded_reason.

request.description:
The shop front: products AND standalone books in ONE list, one shape, one sort.

Every entry carries `item_type` ('product' or 'book'), and the `id` is unique only WITHIN its type. Key on the pair — an id that silently means two different things in two tables is how a cart buys the wrong row.

AUTH IS OPTIONAL. Remove the Authorization header and it still works: a visitor sees what is on sale. Signed in, books additionally carry `own` and `is_locked`.

`statistics` splits the count into products and books.

Products without the books.

Useful for telling the two sources apart while checking a number that looks wrong — `/store` returning more than you expect is usually both kinds counted together.
Sorted on `effective_price`, so a discounted product sorts at what it actually costs rather than at its list price.

query.description: Drop categories with no live products.

request.description:
The active product categories a shopper may browse, each with `products_count` — how many live products it holds, so the shop front can hide an empty shelf instead of opening one.

NO AUTH. Names come back in the request's language (`Accept-Language`), falling back to any translation and then to the code.

query.description: Or by slug, which is what a public URL would carry.

request.description:
One product, in the same shape the store list uses. Takes `id` OR `slug`.

ONLY a live, visible product — this is the shopper's view, not the admin's. An inactive or hidden product returns "not found" rather than a card nobody should see.

The attachment is described (`has_file`, `file_name`, `file_extension`, `file_size_label`) but `file_path` comes back ONLY when `file_is_public` is 1.

NO AUTH.
